70s_1: Queen's scientists determined this song is the most 'feel-good' song ever recorded based on tempo and key.
70s_2: This was the only ABBA song to reach #1 on the US Billboard Hot 100 chart.
70s_3: The beat of this song (103 BPM) is used to train proper chest compression rates for CPR.
70s_4: The date mentioned in the opening line, '21st night of September', was chosen simply because it sounded best.
70s_5: Originally released as a B-side, this became an anthem of empowerment and one of the biggest disco hits ever.
70s_6: Written in 15 minutes, this song was directly inspired by the lead singer's crush on a girl named Sharona.
70s_7: The 'Y.M.C.A.' dance with the arm movements didn't exist until the audience on 'American Bandstand' started doing it.
70s_8: This was the first rock-disco fusion song, winning the first-ever Grammy for Best Rock Vocal Performance, Female.
70s_9: Originally a slower reggae track, it was transformed into a disco hit that even punk clubs played.
70s_10: This was the first solo single Michael Jackson wrote himself, marking his creative independence.
70s_11: The group Sister Sledge really were four sisters, making the chorus 'I've got all my sisters with me' literal.
70s_12: The frantic violin solo was played by Charlie Daniels himself, who overdubbed it seven times to sound like a 'band of demons'.
70s_13: The 'Highway to Hell' was actually the nickname the band gave to their grueling tour schedule.
70s_14: This 14-minute track is widely credited as the first hip-hop song to achieve mainstream success.
70s_15: The Bee Gees wrote this for the 'Saturday Night Fever' soundtrack without even seeing the movie first.
70s_16: Barry Gibb of the Bee Gees wrote this title track, providing backing vocals that sound like his own songs.
70s_17: Bobby Farrell, the male performer, didn't actually sing on the record; the vocals were by producer Frank Farian.
70s_18: Freddie Mercury wrote this anthem specifically to involve the audience, encouraging them to sing along.
70s_19: Written as a birthday gift for his first wife, Elizabeth Weber, who also managed his business.
70s_20: The vocoded voice at the end says 'Please turn me over', instructing listeners to flip the vinyl record.
70s_21: This collaboration with The Emotions was a massive hit, blending Earth, Wind & Fire's funk with disco.
70s_22: The iconic saxophone riff was almost played on a guitar because the sax player, Raphael Ravenscroft, was late.
70s_23: The famous breakdown 'Freak out!' was originally a profanity directed at Studio 54's doormen who rejected them.
70s_24: Debbie Harry wrote this about a real-life stalker she had before she was famous.
70s_25: The stomping and clapping beat was designed to be performed by a crowd without needing instruments.
70s_26: The lyrics are a metaphorical description of the excess and self-destruction of the music industry in Hollywood.
70s_27: David Bowie was inspired to write this after seeing his producer kissing his backing singer by the Berlin Wall.
70s_28: Lindsey Buckingham wrote this angry breakup song about bandmate Stevie Nicks, who had to sing backing vocals on it.
70s_29: Stevie Nicks wrote this in about 10 minutes in a studio next door while the band argued.
70s_30: The aggressive galloping rhythm was created as a reaction to a creepy ad suggesting the Wilson sisters were lovers.
70s_31: Brian Eno declared this track 'the sound of the future' due to its fully synthesized backing track.
70s_32: The song took 5 years to complete, with Tom Scholz working in his basement studio to perfect the sound.
70s_33: Bob Marley wrote this during his exile in London, hoping for peace between rival political factions in Jamaica.
70s_34: The band didn't know the plot of the movie 'Saturday Night Fever' when they wrote this soul ballad for it.
70s_35: Elton John sang this playful duet live with Kiki Dee at Live Aid in 1985.
70s_36: The original lyrics were set in 1933 against the backdrop of Prohibition, not 1963.
70s_37: The band was a white rock group who wrote this after being told by a club audience to 'play some funky music'.
70s_38: The iconic 'more cowbell' sketch on SNL made this song famous to a new generation, although the cowbell is actually quite subtle.
70s_39: The spacey sound effects were created with a synthesizer, marking a shift towards more futuristic rock production.
70s_40: This was ABBA's biggest selling single of all time, with over 10 million physical copies sold.
70s_41: This disco hit features a unique tempo change, starting slow and sultry before exploding into an upbeat groove.
70s_42: Written as a tribute to jazz legend Duke Ellington, who had passed away shortly before its release.
70s_43: The lyrics consist of only six different words repeated throughout the entire song.
70s_44: The deep male voice is actually producer Frank Farian electronically pitched down; he also sang the falsetto parts.
70s_45: At the time, this was the most expensive single ever made and record executives feared it was too long for radio.
70s_46: Neil Sedaka, who wrote the song, originally recorded it as a ballad before the Captain & Tennille made it upbeat.
70s_47: Written about a veteran Broadway star, it became a massive crossover hit for both country and pop charts.
70s_48: John Lennon provided the backing vocals and guitar riff, co-writing the song with Bowie in a jam session.
70s_49: Inspired by Maurice White's thoughts on looking up to the stars for spiritual guidance and hope.
70s_50: The rhythm was inspired by the sound of the band's car driving across a bridge into Miami.
70s_51: This became the first disco song to reach #1 on the Billboard Hot 100.
70s_52: The title came from a line in the movie 'Young Frankenstein' that the band members loved quoting.
70s_53: Stevie Nicks wrote this about deciding whether to go back to school or continue with music.
70s_54: The unique saxophone line was actually played by all three sax players in the band simultaneously.
70s_55: The 'Ooga-Chaka' chant was originally from a 1959 recording and was added to give the cover a jungle feel.
70s_56: Despite sounding like a Swamp Rock band from Louisiana, Redbone was actually a Native American band from California.
70s_57: Live crowd noise was added to the studio recording to simulate a concert atmosphere.
70s_58: The term 'pompatus of love' is a made-up word that Steve Miller lifted from an old R&B song.
70s_59: This song won the Eurovision Song Contest in 1974, launching ABBA's international career.
70s_60: Written as a response to Neil Young's songs 'Southern Man' and 'Alabama' which criticized the South.
70s_61: The grunting vocals and jungle sounds were performed by the band's roadie, 'Don't-Ask-Me'.
70s_62: This was one of the first commercially successful songs to use a drum machine (a Roland Rhythm 77).
70s_63: Barry White's deep voice and romantic lyrics made this a definitive song for 70s bedroom soul.
70s_64: Freddie Mercury said this song was about a high-class call girl, written in a 'vaudeville' style.
70s_65: Elton John's first US #1 hit, inspired by the Australian band Daddy Cool's hit 'Eagle Rock'.
70s_66: The famous clavinet riff was created by Stevie Wonder; Jeff Beck created the drum beat.
70s_67: The cash register loop was handmade by Roger Waters splicing pieces of tape together.
70s_68: Originally written as a religious song, Marvin Gaye transformed it into a sexually charged anthem.
70s_69: Roberta Flack heard this song on a plane and loved it so much she tracked down the writer to record it.
70s_70: Wait, 'Smoke on the Water'? That riff is the first thing every guitar student learns! Also, it's about a real casino fire in Montreux.
70s_71: The characters in the song (John the bartender, Paul the novelist) were real people Billy Joel met while working at a piano bar.
70s_72: Originally titled 'Midnight Plane to Houston', but changed because a 'train into Georgia' sounded more romantic.
70s_73: Steven Tyler wrote this song years before the band formed, using money he found in a suitcase.
70s_74: Dolly Parton wrote 'Jolene' and 'I Will Always Love You' on the very same day.
70s_75: The 'day the music died' refers to the 1959 plane crash that killed Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens, and The Big Bopper.
70s_76: Bill Withers wrote this simple song on a Wurlitzer electric piano about his childhood community.
70s_77: Produced by the same team as David Bowie's 'Space Oddity', exploring similar themes of isolation in space.
70s_78: The song was banned by some US radio stations because 'horse' was thought to be slang for heroin.
70s_79: James Taylor and Linda Ronstadt provided the backing vocals for this acoustic hit.
70s_80: Al Green wrote the lyrics in 15 minutes after a show, capturing a spiritual and romantic plea.
70s_81: The opening bassline is one of the most famous in history; the full album version runs for nearly 12 minutes.
70s_82: Based on a real urban legend or just a story? The band says it's about a spinster named Mary Ellis in New Jersey.
70s_83: Tom Johnston wrote this as a call for world peace, believing music could solve conflict.
70s_84: Produced by David Bowie, this song features a groundbreaking double bass solo.
70s_85: Contrary to rumors, the band claims the song was not written containing hidden satanic messages when played backwards.
70s_86: John Lennon described this as 'virtually the Communist Manifesto' but sugar-coated so it would be accepted.
70s_87: The saxophone intro was actually an accident—the sax player was just warming up, but they kept it.
70s_88: The mandolin part plays the same riff throughout the entire song because the player didn't know technically how to change it.
70s_89: The repeated 'I know, I know' line was a placeholder lyric Bill Withers intended to change, but others convinced him to keep it.
70s_90: The synthesizer intro was generated by feeding personal data of the band's guru, Meher Baba, into a computer.
70s_91: Bernie Taupin wrote the lyrics about his first wife, Maxine Feibelman, who was the band's seamstress.
70s_92: John Denver had never even been to West Virginia when he recorded this song.
70s_93: This was the first #1 hit to feature a drum machine instead of a live drummer.
70s_94: Eddie Kendricks' vocals were so high that many listeners initially thought a woman was singing lead.
70s_95: Art Garfunkel initially didn't want to sing it, thinking Paul Simon should, but Simon insisted.
70s_96: Paul McCartney wrote this after having a dream about his late mother, Mary, who told him 'it will be alright'.
70s_97: The guitar riff was improvised on stage during a concert when the band realized they didn't have an encore prepared.
70s_98: Originally a Temptations song, Edwin Starr recorded the most famous version with a harder, psychedelic soul edge.
70s_99: This was the fourth consecutive #1 hit for the Jackson 5, a record at the time.
70s_100: The song was written as a filler track in under 30 minutes because they needed one more song for the album.
70s_101: The lyrics were controversial for the time, detailing a romantic encounter with a trans woman.
70s_102: This is a cover of a Fleetwood Mac song, but Santana's version became far more famous.
70s_103: Elton John wrote the music in 20 minutes after Bernie Taupin handed him the lyrics over breakfast.
70s_104: The rhythmic sound is Paul Simon hitting his leg, recorded on a tape loop.
